Paper_name: Indistinguishable behavioural and neural correlates of perceptual self-other distinction in autistic and neurotypical adults
Summary: This study tested whether self-bias and familiarity effects in a perceptual face-label matching task are atypical in autism spectrum conditions (ASC). Participants distinguished face-label associations of the self from those of other people of differing familiarity (friend vs stranger). Experiment 1 took an individual differences approach (neurotypical adults, N = 59); Experiment 2 took a case-control approach comparing neurotypical (N = 27) and autistic (N = 30) adults while recording event-related potentials (N1, N2, P3). Across both experiments, behavioural self-bias (self > friend and stranger) and familiarity effects (friend > stranger) were observed and were unaffected by autistic traits or diagnosis. In Experiment 2, both groups showed a typical self-bias in the ERP components, and only the autistic group showed evidence of a familiarity effect (N2 more negative-going for stranger than friend).
Author: Marchella Smith, Heather J. Ferguson
Conclusion: Behavioural and neural correlates of perceptual self-other distinction are indistinguishable between autistic and neurotypical adults, with the findings discussed in relation to self-other distinction ability and other conditions such as anxiety and alexithymia.
